source_text: Haereat igitur hoc maxime prudentis animo lectoris, omnibus Scripturis sacris solum illud, quod in honorem Dei Catholici sapiunt, contineri, sicut frequentium sententiarum luce illustratur; et sicubi durior elocutio moverit quaestionem, certum quidem esse, non ibi id, quod iniustum est, loci illius auctorem sapuisse; secundum id autem debere intellegi, quod et ratio perspicua, et aliorum locorum, in quibus non est ambiguitas, splendor aperuerit. Iam igitur eius cum quo agimus verba ponamus. Equidem in illo capite dictorum suorum, quod usque ad figulum peccatorum Deum suum adduxerat, contra quod libro superiore confliximus, tenuiter dixit, per unum hominem peccatum intrasse in mundum; non est autem in expositione loci ipsius immoratus. Postquam vero multis verbis contra illa excerpta, quae ad se confirmat missa, disseruit, pervenit ad aliquem dictorum meorum locum, quem sibi quasi oppugnaturus obiecit; sed nihil secundum id quod fuerat pulsatus referens, ad hanc Apostoli sententiam convolavit, in qua dicit, per unum hominem peccatum intrasse in mundum; et secundum dogma suum, contextum loci ipsius exponere molitus est; propter quod ego, praetermissis aliis, ad eam properavi partem, ut quia me promiseram hanc esse quaestionem in secundo volumine soluturum [n22] , et fidem promissionis implerem, et argumentatio illius quae esset ostenderem, ne putarer fecisse fraudem, si illius expositione suppressa, eam quam catholicam fatemur inferrem.
pass_a_gloss: Let this therefore especially cling to the mind of a prudent reader, that in all the sacred Scriptures only that is contained which catholics understand unto the honor of God, as it is illustrated by the light of frequent sentences; and if anywhere a harder elocution has moved a question, it is certain indeed that the author of that place did not mean there that which is unjust; but that it ought to be understood according to that which both clear reason and the splendor of other places in which there is not ambiguity have opened. Now therefore let us set down the words of him with whom we deal. Indeed in that head of his sayings which had brought his God even to a potter of sinners, against which we fought in the earlier book, he said thinly that through one human being sin entered into the world; but he did not linger in the exposition of the place itself. But after he discussed with many words against those excerpts which he affirms were sent to him, he came to some place of my sayings, which he threw up to himself as if about to attack it; but bringing back nothing according to that by which he had been struck, he flew together to this sentence of the Apostle, in which he says that through one human being sin entered into the world; and according to his own dogma he attempted to explain the texture of the place itself; on account of which I, other things having been passed by, have hurried to that part, so that, because I had promised that I would solve this question in the second volume, I might both fulfill the faith of the promise and show what that argumentation of his was, lest I be thought to have made a fraud if, his exposition having been suppressed, I brought in that which we confess as catholic.

pass_b_english: Above all, then, let the discerning reader hold firmly to this: all sacred Scripture contains only what catholics understand to honor God, as the light of its many statements makes clear. If a difficult expression raises a question, it is certain that the passage’s author did not intend anything unjust. It must be understood in accordance with what clear reason and the brilliance of other, unambiguous passages have disclosed. Let us now set down the words of our opponent. In that part of his argument where he had brought his God to the point of being a potter of sinners—the argument we opposed in the preceding book—he briefly said that sin entered the world through one man, without dwelling on the passage’s explanation (Romans 5:12). After many words against the excerpts he says were sent to him, however, he reached a passage of mine which he set before himself as though to attack it. Yet he offered nothing that answered the attack made on him. Instead, he took refuge in the apostle’s statement that sin entered the world through one man, and tried to explain the passage’s whole sequence in accordance with his own doctrine. For this reason I have passed over other matters and hurried to this part. Since I promised to resolve this question in the second book, I wanted both to keep that promise and to show what his argument actually was. Otherwise I might be thought dishonest for suppressing his explanation and supplying the one we acknowledge as catholic (see Against Julian, Unfinished Work 1.113).
